source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Prompted LLMs are weak at filling frame roles (frame elements) from text. Fine-tuned open models beat the old best systems.
numbers: Few-shot F1 on FrameNet frame-element identification: GPT-4o-mini 0.471, DeepSeek V3 0.548, GPT-4o 0.592. Prior fine-tuned systems: KID 0.756, AGED 0.767, Ai&Tu 0.771, KAF-SPA 0.813. LoRA Qwen2.5-72B reached 0.794.
quote: LLMs still struggle with out-of-domain data
limits: English FrameNet only; GPT-4o not fine-tuned; paper text and table margins disagree slightly.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only role filling is not reliable. Our S1/S2 frame step needs a code check or a human-checkable output, not a trusted model judgment.

source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Output format changes accuracy a lot. A JSON frame listing only the frame elements that exist in the sentence worked best; XML tags worst.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini few-shot F1: XML-tag 0.342, JSON-all (all possible roles listed) 0.440, Markdown 0.448, JSON-exist 0.471. Gap XML to JSON-exist 12.9 F1 points.
limits: Single model for this ablation. Showing all possible roles raises recall (0.577) but hurts precision (0.356): the model invents fillers for roles that are absent.
agent_relevance: When the agent writes a task frame, use a JSON form and let it mark roles as absent. Listing every role invites made-up fillers (over-prediction).

source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Fine-tuned models lose most when the roles themselves are new, less when only the frame is new. Out-of-domain text is hard.
numbers: Fine-tuned Phi-4 F1: all test 0.785; unseen frames 0.708 (-7.7); unseen frame elements 0.515 (-27.0). On YAGS out-of-domain: GPT-4o 0.387, Phi-4 0.533, SEMAFOR 0.570.
quote: frame-semantic knowledge may not be sufficiently encoded
limits: Many YAGS roles are not in FrameNet and some annotation is doubtful. Only seed 0 for tie-breaks.
agent_relevance: A frame the model has not seen is a weak scaffold. Role names must be given in the prompt, not assumed from memory.

source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Training-data size scaling and frame identification side result.
numbers: Phi-4 F1 rose from 0.508 at 1% of data to 0.785 at 100%; flattened after 50% (0.766). Frame identification on ambiguous targets 0.862 vs CoFFTEA 0.850, but overall 0.894 below KGFI 0.924 and CoFFTEA 0.926.
limits: State-of-the-art claim holds only for ambiguous targets.
agent_relevance: Small tuned models can match big prompted ones on frame tasks; but our scaffold is training-free, so this is a ceiling, not an option.

source: Garat, Moncecchi, Wonsever (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: With FrameNet definitions and examples placed in the prompt, six LLMs identify frames and targets very well on a 6-frame violence subset.
numbers: Best F1 frame/target: Haiku 3.5 91.8/90.9, Sonnet 3.5 94.0/93.1, DeepSeek Chat 95.3/94.3 (100 shots), DeepSeek Reasoner 94.4/93.5, GPT-4o-mini 92.4/91.0, GPT-4o 93.8/92.9. Gain from more shots only 1.4 to 8.7 points.
limits: Only 6 frames chosen for prompt size; 100 test examples, one frame per example; exact-span scoring; paper has version typos (Haiku 3.7 vs 3.5).
agent_relevance: Giving the model the frame definition and examples works for choosing the frame. Cheap in an S1 step.

source: Garat, Moncecchi, Wonsever (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Filling the roles is harder than picking the frame, and errors compound when the frame is predicted rather than given.
numbers: Argument identification F1 with gold frames: Haiku 68.9, Sonnet 76.3, DeepSeek Chat 72.3, DeepSeek Reasoner 77.4, GPT-4o-mini 67.1, GPT-4o 73.9. With predicted frames: Haiku 53.5, Sonnet 68.6, GPT-4o-mini 53.2, Reasoner 74.9. Killing frame full parse: Sonnet 82.9, GPT-4o 80.2, Haiku 71.1, GPT-4o-mini 68.7.
limits: Authors say direct comparison with fine-tuned systems (about 75.6 to 77.1 F1) is not feasible. Rare roles weak: Means and Instrument at or below 50.0 even for the best model.
agent_relevance: Peripheral roles (means, instrument, place) are exactly the ones the model misses. Empty-role checks should target them with explicit questions.

source: Garat, Moncecchi, Wonsever (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Frame information in the prompt matters most for role filling. Without it, some models score near zero.
numbers: Zero-shot FSRL F1 no frame info / definition only / all frame info: GPT-4o-mini 3.9 / 36.4 / 39.3; Haiku 22.2 / 33.0 / 32.4; DeepSeek Chat 28.0 / 42.4 / 44.6; GPT-4o 25.6 / 32.1 / 39.5. Full parse on Killing zero-shot: 0.0 with no info or definition only; 34.1 to 48.4 with all info. Frame ID zero-shot: GPT-4o 74.1 no info vs 90.7 all info.
limits: Strong models (DeepSeek) already know frames without help (frame ID 90.4 without info). Effect depends on model.
agent_relevance: Supports writing the role list into the prompt (a frame template), not asking the model to recall it. Large gain for weaker models.

source: Chundru, Poddar, Cao, Jiang (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: A small open model with lightweight prompts picks the right FrameNet frame most of the time, but trails supervised systems. Tuning closes the gap.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct accuracy FN1.5 / FN1.7: simple zero-shot 82.4 / 80.0; Direct-QA few-shot 83.3 / 83.5; QA fine-tuned 91.7 / 91.9. Supervised SOTA: COFFTEA 92.5 / 92.6, Tamburini 92.5 / 92.3. 3 runs average.
limits: Frame names given as options (multiple choice), not open recall. Single model family for most tests.
agent_relevance: Choosing among named frames is easy when options are offered. Offer a menu of candidate frames rather than asking for open recall.

source: Chundru, Poddar, Cao, Jiang (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Prompt ingredients matter: showing frame names alone zero-shot is poor in the 'simple' format; a multiple-choice 'Direct-QA' format is robust.
numbers: FN1.7 zero-shot / few-shot: Simple frame names only 59.9 / 79.1; Simple names plus lexical-unit definitions 76.2 / 79.8; Direct-QA names only 80.1 / 81.3; Direct-QA names plus LU definitions 80.8 / 83.5. Other models few-shot: Llama 75.4, DeepSeek-V3.1 79.1, GPT-4o 80.1 (another table).
limits: Differences of 1 to 3 points are within the 3-run noise range in places.
agent_relevance: Adding a sense definition of the key word is worth about 1 to 3 points; format (lettered choices) is worth up to 20 points in the weakest prompt.

source: Chundru, Poddar, Cao, Jiang (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Out of domain, zero-shot models are weaker; tuning lifts YAGS a lot but entity-style 'Artifacts' data stays hard. LLM-written frame definitions work about as well as gold ones.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B on YAGS: zero-shot 65.4, QA fine-tuned 80.7 (FIDO 70.5, Hartmann 62.5). Artifacts: 25.6 to 49.6. Error overlap with FIDO: 296 agreeing wrong predictions, 24 disagreeing, 320 common wrong of about 519 to 538. LLM-generated definitions gave accuracy comparable to gold definitions.
quote: LLMs encode frame-semantic knowledge and can serve as effective solutions
limits: Authors say the Artifacts set is phrase-level and tests abstraction; fine-tuned model still below 50 there. Llama family only.
agent_relevance: The model can write its own frame definition at about gold quality, so an agent can build a frame on the fly (S1) without a lookup table.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2025) Injecting Frame Semantics into LLMs via Prompt-Based Fine-Tuning
finding: Injecting frame knowledge by LoRA on 50 FrameNet frames helps on frame questions and on a quick role-labeling test, even for 10 frames held out.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B closed-ended F1 in/out 0.93/0.87 (adapted); open-ended cosine 0.55/0.52 to 0.87/0.73; MCQ F1 0.27/0.34 to 0.91/0.86. Llama-3.2-3B baseline unseen frames: MCQ F1 0.33, open cosine 0.63.
limits: Only 50 frames trained, 10 unseen. Base closed-ended F1 values are partly garbled in the extracted table; check the PDF before quoting small cells.
agent_relevance: Base models do poorly on role and definition questions about frames; so an agent prompt should supply role lists itself.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2025) Injecting Frame Semantics into LLMs via Prompt-Based Fine-Tuning
finding: Zero-shot SRL on OpenSesame: tuned model recovers far more roles but spans stay loose.
numbers: 371 sentences, 468 instances, 38 of 50 frames. Roles-only F1 0.14 base vs 0.60 tuned; roles+span 25% overlap 0.41 tuned; 75% overlap 0.10 base vs 0.25 tuned (0.07 base at the strictest). Cited ChatGPT PropBank few-shot F1: 0.40 (CoNLL-05 WSJ), 0.38 (CoNLL-12), zero-shot 0.22 (Cheng et al. 2024).
limits: Not comparable to dedicated SRL systems; subset of frames; PropBank vs FrameNet differ.
agent_relevance: Role labels are easier than exact spans. Frames should name roles loosely, with short filler phrases rather than exact spans.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2026) Frame-Semantic Knowledge Injection for Event-Level Inference in LLMs
finding: Frame knowledge over the full FrameNet (1,200+ frames) helps natural language inference about events, most for entailment and contradiction.
numbers: CONFER (2.3k items) accuracy zero-shot / few-shot: base Llama-3.1-8B 0.52 / 0.39; FrameNet-adapted 0.55 / 0.75; GPT-OSS-20B 0.39 / 0.39; Gemma-2B 0.30 / 0.44. Entailment zero-shot 0.10 to 0.55. SNLI diagnostic few-shot 0.73 to 0.77; random 20k SNLI 0.74 to 0.76. LU F1 0.50 to 0.62, frame F1 0.66 to 0.81.
limits: 8B model, tuning not prompting; SNLI gain is small (0.02 to 0.04); neutral zero-shot got worse (0.56 to 0.33 on subset); no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Gains are real but small outside frame-triggered items. Frames help event logic more than general reasoning; do not oversell as a general reasoning boost.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2026) Frame-Semantic Knowledge Injection for Event-Level Inference in LLMs
finding: Few-shot examples hurt the base model on CONFER (0.52 to 0.39) but not the frame-tuned one. Strict span matching stays low.
numbers: Roles+Span at 50% overlap 0.13 base vs 0.21 adapted; 100% overlap 0.11 vs 0.20. Adapted beats GPT-OSS-20B by 0.36 few-shot with 12B fewer parameters.
limits: Own run of GPT-OSS-20B; counterintuitive drop matches the original CONFER paper for some models.
agent_relevance: Few-shot demos are not always safe; test each scaffold element against a no-scaffold baseline (G-rule on controls).

source: Iwamoto, Ohara (2026) FrameNet annotations added to LLM prompts for commonsense multiple choice (ANLP 2026, Japanese)
finding: Adding FrameNet frame names and frame elements to the prompt raised accuracy on SWAG next-situation choice. WordNet sense tags helped about as much.
numbers: SWAG 5000-item test, GPT-4o-mini: baseline 75.2 plus or minus 0.3; FrameNet-annotated variants about 79.5 to 80.3; WordNet variant 80.3 plus or minus 0.6. GPT-5 mini 80.9 to 84.9; Llama-3.3-70B 76.3 to 79.3 (row pairing read from garbled text). A second set: 83.2 to 85.2 (FrameNet) vs 84.7 (WordNet).
limits: Japanese PDF text extracted with broken characters; I could read numbers but not all labels, so row pairing is partly inferred. Not peer reviewed (author statement). Frames came from an automatic T5 parser, not gold. FrameNet did not beat WordNet.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that frame labels in the prompt add roughly 4 to 5 points on situation choice for small-to-mid models. A plain lexical sense tag gave the same gain, so the benefit may be generic 'more structure', not frame theory.

source: Han, Sasano, Takeda (2024) Definition Generation for Automatically Induced Semantic Frame
finding: Chain-of-thought that first lists the frame elements makes generated frame definitions name more correct roles, with no loss in overall definition quality.
numbers: Llama-2-70b-chat. FE-Eval 0.69 (word list + exemplars) vs 0.79 to 0.80 with FE reasoning; Def-Eval (GPT-4 judge, 1 to 5) 3.40 vs 3.43 to 3.44. Demonstrations: 0 shots 2.67, 1 shot 2.96, 3 shots 3.43 or so, 5 shots 3.59, 10 shots 3.42. QLoRA fine-tuning 3.62 about the same as 5-shot ICL.
limits: One model; judge is GPT-4 (correlation with humans better than BLEU but BERTScore only 0.13); Japanese or other languages not tested.
agent_relevance: This is a frame-element step used inside prompting: listing the roles first improves role coverage by about 10 points. A direct template for S1.

source: Vijayvargiya et al. (2026) Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering (ICLR 2026)
finding: Agents rarely notice that a task has empty roles. When they do ask, success rises a lot. Not frame-based, but it tests the same step: spot missing information.
numbers: Interaction raises resolve rate on underspecified issues by up to 74% over non-interactive. Only Claude Sonnet 4 (89%) and Sonnet 3.5 (84%) separate well-specified from underspecified inputs well; Qwen 3 Coder 100% false-negative rate (chance, 50%). Interaction recovers up to 80% of the lost performance for some models.
quote: models struggle to distinguish between well-specified and underspecified instructions
limits: Underspecified issues are synthetic (GPT-4o rewrites); user is simulated; without explicit prompting models almost never ask.
agent_relevance: Strongest case for an explicit empty-role check in code, since models do not ask on their own. Frames give the checklist of what to ask about.

source: Edwards, Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents
finding: A separate monitor agent that checks every turn for gaps and forces a question lifts resolve rate to near fully-specified level.
numbers: 500 SWE-bench Verified issues made underspecified. Claude Sonnet 4.5 resolve: UA-Multi 69.40, UA-Single 61.20, fully specified 70.80 (UA-Multi vs FULL p=0.458). Kimi K2.6: 69.40, 61.60, 72.80. Cost per task Claude 3.50 vs 2.03 dollars. Asked in 344 of 500 tasks.
limits: Scaffold effect confounded with extra calls and prompt design; synthetic gaps; simulated user; two models. Subset comparison self-selected. Opened via a summary page, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Matches our design: the program, not the model, owns the gap check (a separate checker pass beat a self-reminder by about 8 points).

source: Das, Chen, Martins, Schneider, Smith (2014) Frame-Semantic Parsing (SEMAFOR)
finding: Classic statistical frame parser. Frame identification is good, argument filling is the weak step, and errors carry over from frame to role.
numbers: FrameNet 1.5 frame ID with gold targets: 82.97 F1 exact, 90.51 partial. Ambiguous targets (50.1% of test): 73.10 exact, 85.77 partial accuracy. Predicted frames cost 22 points of argument F1 (18 with partial credit). Beat the SemEval-2007 baseline by more than 4.4 F1.
limits: 2014 data and features; different FrameNet release from LLM papers; scores not directly comparable with LLM studies.
agent_relevance: Same shape as the LLM results 10 years later: frame choice easy, role filling hard. Pipeline errors compound.

source: Swayamdipta, Thomson, Dyer, Smith (2017) Frame-Semantic Parsing with Softmax-Margin Segmental RNNs and a Syntactic Scaffold
finding: Neural frame parser (Open-SESAME) with a training-time syntactic scaffold task matched the state of the art without a parser at test time.
numbers: Frame+argument ID, predicted frames F1: SEMAFOR 66.8, FitzGerald 2015 67.9, ensemble 69.9; Open-SESAME 70.2 to 70.9 variants, scaffold 68.0, scaffold ensemble 69.3. Best scaffold model within 0.2 absolute F1 of state of the art.
limits: Scaffold gain small; numbers from my read of a partly garbled table, check before reuse. FrameNet 1.5 era.
agent_relevance: Prior art for 'scaffold' meaning auxiliary training task, not prompt scaffold. Do not confuse the two uses of the word.

source: Gildea, Jurafsky (2002) Automatic Labeling of Semantic Roles
finding: First statistical FrameNet role labeler. Role identification works when segments are given; the full task is much harder.
numbers: 82% accuracy on role of presegmented constituents (80.4% final system vs 40.9% always choosing the most probable role); with segmentation, 65% precision and 61% recall. 13% of frame elements had no matching parse constituent. Frame-specific roles 80.4% vs abstract thematic roles 82.1%.
limits: Early FrameNet release; parser errors drive part of the loss.
agent_relevance: Shows frame-specific roles are no harder than generic roles; supports a frame-per-task design rather than one fixed role list.

source: Kabbach (2019) Debugging Frame Semantic Role Labeling
finding: Replication on FrameNet 1.7 shows that preprocessing (dependency parser choice) changes argument identification scores as much as new models claim to gain.
numbers: Reports gains from preprocessing of the same order as recent model gains; cites 20 F1 loss out of domain (Johansson and Nugues 2007) and Das 2014's finding that exemplar sentences did not help. Kshirsagar 2015 and Yang & Mitchell 2017 saw only a few F1 points from exemplars.
limits: Thesis; exact table numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Small reported gains in this literature may be pipeline artifacts. Require same-input, same-seed controls before believing a frame effect.

source: Su et al. (2024) in-context learning for argument identification with Llama 2 (cited in Devasier 2025)
finding: Cited as an early test of in-context frame argument identification; reported very poor performance with a simple prompt on Llama 2.
numbers: No numbers read. Described only through Devasier et al. 2025 and a search summary.
limits: Not opened; the primary paper was not found.
agent_relevance: Baseline for how weak simple prompting was before structured prompts and bigger models.

source: Cheng et al. (2024) semantic role labeling with ChatGPT (PropBank; cited by Rai 2025)
finding: Cited as showing a big gap between ChatGPT and trained SRL systems on PropBank.
numbers: As quoted by Rai et al.: ChatGPT 3-shot F1 0.40 (CoNLL-2005 WSJ), 0.38 (CoNLL-2012 WSJ), 0.22 zero-shot (CoNLL-2005). Search summary also mentioned GPT-4 42.9% few-shot on a PropBank study; not verified.
limits: Not opened. PropBank, not FrameNet.
agent_relevance: Role labeling by prompt was weak in 2024; later 2025 results with frame info in the prompt are better.

source: Requirements generation guided by FrameNet roles (AAAI Spring Symposium paper)
finding: A search summary says FrameNet core and non-core frame elements were used to find missing semantic roles and steer an LLM when writing requirements; completeness and efficiency improved over a plain prompt.
numbers: No numbers obtained: the page was blocked by a bot filter.
limits: Not opened; claim comes from a search result summary only.
agent_relevance: The closest found use of frame-element gap finding inside an LLM generation loop. Retrieve the paper before relying on it.

source: NoisyToolBench / Ask-when-Needed (EMNLP 2025) and ClarifyBench (2025)
finding: Search summaries: agents tend to invent missing tool arguments; asking when needed reduces this. These are slot-filling style tests of missing roles.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; titles from a search result only.
agent_relevance: Tool-call arguments are frame roles in disguise; the missing-argument check is the same operation.

source: Bobrow et al. (1977) GUS, a frame-driven dialog system (older AI system, not opened)
finding: Frame-based dialog manager: a frame has slots, the system keeps asking for unfilled slots until done. Search results described a modern patent version of the same loop.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; only referenced via search summary of a related patent. Slot-frame (Minsky) lineage, not Fillmore's FrameNet.
agent_relevance: The oldest working example of 'ask for empty roles' in a loop. Our S1/S2 step is this with an LLM.
